History

Portable dry-herb vaporizers descend from desktop convection machines such as the Volcano, miniaturised once lithium-ion batteries and precise temperature controllers became small enough to carry. Early portables used simple conduction ovens with preset temperatures; later models added hybrid conduction-convection heating, digital displays, and phone apps. The PAX line is a well-known example of the pocket form: a slim metal body, a small oven, and a mouthpiece, with heat modes stepped from about 374 F to 428 F. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The portable dry-herb vaporizer works by a battery-powered heater warms a small oven holding ground herb to a set temperature below combustion, and the user draws the released vapour through a mouthpiece. It is made from anodised aluminium or stainless-steel body, ceramic or stainless-steel oven, lithium-ion battery, glass or plastic mouthpiece, and a common example measures 105 mm tall x 32 mm wide; twin-zone oven holds about 0.3 g. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature aluminium body; ceramic twin-zone oven; lithium-ion battery; glass mouthpiece

Dimensions: 105 mm tall x 32 mm wide; twin-zone oven holds about 0.3 g

Mechanism: Twin-zone oven: two separately controlled heater zones warm the herb from both ends at once, so the middle of the load reaches temperature as fast as the edges

Use: Fill the twin-zone oven, set the temperature, wait for the ready signal, then draw slowly

Care: Brush the oven after cooling; clean the mouthpiece; recharge by USB-C

Variants: Pocket twin-zone, standard twin-zone, and long-session twin-zone versions

Science proof

A vaporizer works by phase change without combustion. Heating dried herb raises the temperature of its volatile compounds until they boil off as vapour, while the plant fibre itself stays below its burning point, which sources place above about 230 C. Conduction transfers heat by direct contact between the hot oven wall and the herb, which is fast but can heat unevenly. Convection carries heat in a stream of hot air that passes through the herb, which is slower to start but more even. Hybrid ovens use both. The energy needed is the sensible heat of the herb plus the sensible heat of the oven metal or ceramic: mass times specific heat capacity times temperature rise. A lithium-ion battery stores that energy chemically and releases it as electrical heat through a resistive heater, and a controller cycles the heater on and off to hold the set temperature. Lower set temperatures release lighter, more fragrant compounds first; higher set temperatures release more of the heavier compounds. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo uses the sensible-heat formula Q equals m times c times the temperature rise. The herb mass is 0.3 g, its specific heat capacity is 1.7 joules per gram per degree Celsius, and the rise from 20.0 C to 185.0 C is 165.0 degrees, so the herb heat is the product of those three numbers. The oven is heated as well: 14.0 g of oven material at 0.9 joules per gram per degree over the same rise. Adding the two heats gives the total heat per session in joules, and dividing by 3600 converts it to watt-hours. Dividing the battery energy of 12.0 watt-hours by the watt-hours per session gives the number of sessions per charge. The program prints every step, runs the computation twice, and prints SHA-256 digests so the reader can verify the result is deterministic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Fill the twin-zone oven, set the temperature, wait for the ready signal, then draw slowly Brush the oven after cooling; clean the mouthpiece; recharge by USB-C Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

Design-study label

Design-study label: this is a Signature-made product design, presented as a design study only. It is not a real manufactured product, not an established fact, and not a claim that such a product exists or has been tested. The Signature Ember Pocket Vaporizer is a Signature design, not a real product. No claim is made that it has been manufactured, tested, or sold.

Sources

This Signature record has no public sources, because it is a design study, not a harvested public record. Its numbers come from the design specification in this record. demo.code:
"""Demo: portable vaporizer heating energy — The Portable Dry-Herb Vaporizer."""
import hashlib
def compute():
    herb_g = 0.3; t0 = 20.0; t1 = 185.0; cp = 1.7; battery_wh = 12.0; oven_g = 14.0; oven_cp = 0.9
    q_herb_j = herb_g * cp * (t1 - t0)
    q_oven_j = oven_g * oven_cp * (t1 - t0)
    q_total_j = q_herb_j + q_oven_j
    q_total_wh = q_total_j / 3600.0
    sessions = battery_wh / q_total_wh
    temp_rise_c = t1 - t0
    return {"herb_heat_J": round(q_herb_j, 2), "oven_heat_J": round(q_oven_j, 2), "total_heat_J": round(q_total_j, 2), "total_heat_Wh": round(q_total_wh, 4), "sessions_per_charge": round(sessions, 1), "temp_rise_C": temp_rise_c}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["herb_heat_J", "oven_heat_J", "total_heat_J", "total_heat_Wh", "sessions_per_charge", "temp_rise_C"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

description: The Signature Ember Pocket Vaporizer is a Signature-made design study for portable dry-herb vaporizer, a new design in the Signature Marijuana Supplies Database that reworks the familiar public form with one deliberate change. It keeps the job the same — a battery-powered heater warms a small oven holding ground herb to a set temperature below combustion, and the user draws the released vapour through a mouthpiece — but changes how the parts are arranged, using signature aluminium body; ceramic twin-zone oven; lithium-ion battery; glass mouthpiece. The design is sized at 105 mm tall x 32 mm wide; twin-zone oven holds about 0.3 g, which sets every number in this record, from the volumes and areas in the demo to the scale variants at the end. This record is a design study, not a real manufactured product, and nothing here claims the design has been built, tested, or sold. What it does offer is a complete, checkable design: a full specification, the physics of how it would work, worked arithmetic tied to its own dimensions, a runnable program that computes those numbers, and three boundless scale variants. Readers can follow the design from first principles, repeat the arithmetic by hand, run the program, and see exactly where each number comes from. The Signature edition exists alongside the public edition so the archive holds both what exists in the world and what the Signature system designs next, clearly labelled, so the two are never confused. Like every Signature record, it is filed as a design study, with its own generator and its own file AI, and it marches with the rest of the database toward a million records.

Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.

"""Signature Ember Pocket Vaporizer — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (portable vaporizer heating energy),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for Signature Ember Pocket Vaporizer."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        herb_g = 0.3; t0 = 20.0; t1 = 185.0; cp = 1.7; battery_wh = 12.0; oven_g = 14.0; oven_cp = 0.9
        q_herb_j = herb_g * cp * (t1 - t0)
        q_oven_j = oven_g * oven_cp * (t1 - t0)
        q_total_j = q_herb_j + q_oven_j
        q_total_wh = q_total_j / 3600.0
        sessions = battery_wh / q_total_wh
        temp_rise_c = t1 - t0
        return {"herb_heat_J": round(q_herb_j, 2), "oven_heat_J": round(q_oven_j, 2), "total_heat_J": round(q_total_j, 2), "total_heat_Wh": round(q_total_wh, 4), "sessions_per_charge": round(sessions, 1), "temp_rise_C": temp_rise_c}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()
